card.hook: Here's a hot take: the best photo at Norway's big royal monument isn't of the monument at all. It's of the old stone cross sitting in front of it, which makes a much stronger picture than a wide shot full of houses and industry.
card.stand_here: Stand on Krosshaugen, the small hill with the old stone cross, south of the national monument, on the small hill beside it. Face north so the cross is close to you and the obelisk rises behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the cross with the monument behind it. Switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole mound and obelisk in, or try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the obelisk closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cross, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the grey stone doesn't look flat, and use the gridlines to keep the obelisk upright.
card.best_time: There's no particular time you need. Go whenever suits your day.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Krosshaugen, on the small mound beside the monument next to the old cross, which is the spot with a view back to Haraldshaugen. Use the front camera, widen it if your phone has a wider option, and turn so the monument sits behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an outdoor hill site, reached on foot and free to visit. Check the official site before you go in case of any restrictions.
card.challenge: Get the cross and the obelisk in one shot with the cross on one side, like they're having a quiet chat across the centuries.
card.good_to_know: Haraldshaugen is Norway's national monument to King Harald Fairhair. It was unveiled on 18 July 1872, a thousand years after the Battle of Hafrsfjord, and the obelisk is 17 m tall. It's ringed by memorial stones, including 29 smaller ones, one for each of Norway's historic counties. Tradition says Harald is buried here, but there's no clear archaeological proof.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Krosshaugen, the small hill with the old stone cross, south of the national monument, on the small hill beside it. Face north so the cross is close to you and the obelisk rises behind it.

selfie_spots.detail: on the small mound beside the monument, next to the wooden cross
selfie_spots.why: Pages describe this cross hill as beside the monument with a view back to Haraldshaugen, so it is the only spot found where the monument can sit in the background.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot could be supported. The Harald Fairhair statue near the city park (Byparken, northern end of Haraldsgata) is praised as a photo spot, but the pages describe it as a shot of the statue itself, not with Haraldshaugen behind, so I did not list it. The Krosshaugen claim is inferred: the pages say the cross hill has a view to the monument and sits beside it, but none says a visitor selfie is framed with the monument behind. No page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole monument, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules. No page gives a safety point; the 'windswept' hilltop and 'steep' Risøy bridge mentions are descriptions, not safety advice.

card.hook: This gallery looks like it couldn't stop adding rooms, and that's what makes it fun to photograph. A 1915 family house, a 1978 main building and a 2004 extension all sit side by side above the park.
card.stand_here: Stand about 45 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Havnaberggata, and face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole group of buildings in, then try 1x for a more natural view. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on where the old house meets the newer parts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the walls up with them, so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daytime, when you can see the whole outside of the building clearly.
card.selfie_here: Head into Byparken, the city park across from the gallery, and turn so the gallery is behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to squeeze more building in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any rules on photography inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot that shows all three building stages, then one close-up of the spot where old meets new. Bonus points if you can point to the join.
card.good_to_know: The oldest part is a house from around 1915, built as a home for Lars and Inga Meling. The main building came in 1978, designed by architect David Sandved, and a further extension followed in 2004. The collection includes Edvard Munch, Pablo Picasso and Lars Hertervig, and you don't need to go inside to get a good picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 45 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Havnaberggata, and face north-west.

selfie_spots.name: Byparken (city park opposite the gallery)
selfie_spots.detail: In the park across from the gallery, with the gallery building behind you. The page doesn't name a more precise point inside the park.
selfie_spots.why: A travel listing says the park opposite the gallery offers scenic views and a pleasant photo backdrop, and the gallery overlooks this park.

The Havnaberg viewpoint, opposite Byparken with the Harald Fairhair statue, is named by a page, but no page links it to a gallery backdrop, so I left it out. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules or a safety point for this site. Coordinates from Wikipedia (59°25′7.53″N 5°15′48.91″E) match the position you gave.

card.hook: A museum with no ceiling is a gift for your phone. You can step back and grab a whole building, then wander closer for doors, windows and little objects.
card.stand_here: Stand near Hasseløy bru at the phone icon on the map, about 15 m west of the subject, and face east toward Dokken friluftsmuseum.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole scene. If you're too close to fit a building in, tap zoom 0.5x, and use zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details like doors and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings and line up walls and posts with them so your buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or later in the afternoon looks gentler than midday sun. Check the official site before you go to see what's open.
card.selfie_here: Head into the green central courtyard at Dokken and pose with one of the small historic houses behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the house over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stop on Hasseløy Bridge and ask a passer-by to frame you with the museum buildings in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site to see what can be photographed. If you go inside any building, ask before photographing people or displays.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then find a door or window and fill the frame with it.
card.good_to_know: Dokken friluftsmuseum is an open-air museum in Haugesund, so its buildings and objects are shown outdoors rather than in a gallery. It's ranked third on the Haugesund map. We don't have details on its history or opening arrangements, so the official site is your best bet.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Hasseløy bru at the phone icon on the map, about 15 m west of the subject, and face east toward Dokken friluftsmuseum.

selfie_spots.name: Green courtyard at Dokken (Dokken open-air museum, Brugata 1D)
selfie_spots.detail: In the green central courtyard, posing with one of the small historic houses behind you
selfie_spots.why: Sources describe the courtyard as a green area ringed by small historic buildings, which gives a period backdrop, though none names a specific photo point.

ask_someone_spot.detail: Stop on the bridge and have the passer-by frame you with the museum buildings in view

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot could be supported. No page names a specific photo point inside the museum; the 'photo spots among the buildings' (Fjord Norway) are not located. Visit Norway says the bridge is a place to photograph the museum 'from the sea', so the exact camera position for the passer-by is uncertain; the bridge is named, but the museum may be at a distance. The statue of Harald Fairhair across the bridge looks down over the museum (Cruise Turtle), but that places the museum in front of the visitor, not behind, so I did not use it. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, or any safety point. Opening hours differ between sources (Thursdays only in spring/autumn; daily in summer; closed for the season per some listings), so check before going. The AI selfie stand mentioned in reviews is at The Viking Planet, not at Dokken.

card.hook: Dark red brick, steep gables and pointed windows against a pale sky: Vår Frelsers Church practically poses for you. It's big, bold and right in the middle of Haugesund.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Kaigata, about 85 m south-east of the church, and face north-west. From there you can fit the whole building in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole church, then tap 2x to pick out the gables and pointed windows. Only use 0.5x if you step closer, and keep the church in the middle so the edges don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, tap the brickwork, and if the sky is washing out, slide it a touch darker so the red stays rich.
card.best_time: A pale sky is perfect because it makes the dark brick stand out. On a grey day the even light still gives you a clean, honest record shot.
card.selfie_here: Go to the red brick wall on the Skåregata side (the church is at Skåregata 155). Stand with your back to the wall, close enough that the church fills the frame behind you, and use the front camera. Hold the phone a little high and keep the brick behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The road near the church is busy with tourist traffic, so you may need to wait for a clear shot. Check for traffic before you step into the street. It's a working parish church, so dress respectfully if you go inside. Photography inside is allowed and admission is free.
card.challenge: Find the pointiest gable you can, then frame it so the tip sits right in the top centre of your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Architect Einar Halleland won the design competition in February 1899. The church was built between 1899 and 1901 and consecrated on 6 March 1902. It seats about 850 people. Before it existed, locals went to the nearby Skåre Church, but as Haugesund grew after becoming a town in 1854, residents asked for a church of their own in the centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Kaigata, about 85 m south-east of the church, and face north-west. From there you can fit the whole building in the frame.

selfie_spots.name: Red brick wall of Vår Frelsers Church, Skåregata side
selfie_spots.detail: stand with your back to the church's red brick wall, close enough that the building fills the frame behind you; the church's address is Skåregata 155
selfie_spots.why: The church offers great photo opportunities from several angles, or you can take a portrait using the lovely red brick wall as a background.

card.hook: Plot twist: to photograph Haugesund Teater, you actually point your phone at Festiviteten, the big culture house that holds its main stage. Don't worry, the theatre is inside.
card.stand_here: Stand at the entrance side of Haugesund Rådhus (the town hall). The theatre is about 726 m to the north-west, so turn and face the Festiviteten building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole building and a bit of its surroundings. Tap 2x if you want to pick out the façade without moving. Only use 0.5x for a bold shot, and keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the building up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean, then tap the façade and slide it a little darker at dusk so the lit parts don't turn white.
card.best_time: Aim for dusk, when the building is lit against a darker sky. If the light gets low, switch on night mode and rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold the phone a bit higher than usual, and tuck the building into the background over your shoulder. Take a few, because this is a big solid building and you want it to look straight behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the town hall entrance side. If you want to see a performance or go inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the building perfectly straight and a bit of space around it, then one with a passer-by walking through. Which one tells the better story?
card.good_to_know: Haugesund Teater is the regional theatre for Nord-Rogaland and was set up in 1986. Its main stage is inside the Festiviteten culture house. The theatre also has a smaller stage called HAUT on the Smedasundet waterfront, but that's a separate place and you can't see it from the town hall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the entrance side of Haugesund Rådhus (the town hall). The theatre is about 726 m to the north-west, so turn and face the Festiviteten building.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a photo position for Haugesund Teater, so I have no places to report. The theatre's main venue is HAUT scene at Smedasundet 98, a former power-station building on the quay (per haugesundteater.no and sceneweb.no). Pages about Haraldsgata and Rådhusplassen describe the surrounding streets but do not link any spot to this theatre, so I left them out. The landmark's position (59.41420, 5.26540) should be checked against Smedasundet 98 before any spot is added. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules or a safety point for this location.

card.hook: Here's a church photo with no grand front door in it. You get a plain white wall at the end of an ordinary street, and it looks surprisingly good on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Olav Kyrres gate, about 65 m east of the church, and face west along the street. The church's east wall sits in the background, with the building at Erling Skjalgssons gate 15 on the right edge of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the wall with some street around it. If the street feels tight, tap 0.5x for more building and sky, or try 2x for a closer shot of the roofline and wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls and street edges straight, then tap the white wall and slide it a little darker so it stays crisp white instead of washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights the east wall that faces you. Late afternoon puts the sun behind the church, so the wall can look dark. Soft, cloudy light also works well on white.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, use the front camera at 0.5x and step back so the white wall sits over your shoulder. Tilt the phone slightly up so you get more wall and less pavement.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by inside the churchyard (Skåre kirkegård, Haugevegen 19 B) to shoot toward the church at 0.5x for a wide shot, with you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is public, but check the official site before you go for churchyard access and opening times.
card.challenge: Use the gridlines to make the church wall perfectly straight, then see if you can keep that street line pointing right at it. Bonus points if no parked car sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: Skåre Church was built in 1858 to designs by Christian Heinrich Grosch. It's an octagonal wooden church and seats about 450 people. Written records of the site go back to 1301, and the first church here was a stave church that stood across the street.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Olav Kyrres gate, about 65 m east of the church, and face west along the street. The church's east wall sits in the background, with the building at Erling Skjalgssons gate 15 on the right edge of your frame.

ask_someone_spot.name: Skåre Church churchyard (Skåre kirkegård), Haugevegen 19 B
ask_someone_spot.detail: Inside the churchyard, with the passer-by shooting toward the church for a wide-angle frame. The page shows a wide-angle view taken from the church yard; it does not describe a visitor's pose there.

sources.title: Skåre Kirke (Skåre Church) photo spot, Haugesund

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor should stand with Skåre Church behind them, so selfie_spots is empty rather than guessed. The only photo-spot guide (PhotoHound) lists a wide-angle view from the churchyard and a bust on a plinth across the street, but it does not say the church is in the bust shot, so I did not use the bust. The churchyard suggestion for the passer-by rests on a single contributor's photo, and the page does not say where exactly the photographer stood. The Haugesund walking-tour tip about standing across the street to shoot from below refers to Vår Frelsers Kirke (Our Saviour's Church), not Skåre, so I excluded it. Church address is Haugevegen 19 B; the interior is reported as not visitable (Komoot), and no page gives selfie-stick or tripod rules.
